newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan upbeat on economy but warns on wages.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan upbeat on economy but warns on wages.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Tuesday gave an upbeat assessment of the economy but warned of the risks of wage-driven inflation.
Greenspan said wages had been held down by heightened job insecurity but added that he saw signs that that might be coming to an end.
The central bank chairman, in testimony to Congress, also described the rise in the stock market as "breathtaking."

But his remarks, prepared for the Senate Budget Committee, barely had any effect on financial markets Tuesday, unlike in December, when his comment about "irrational exuberance" sparked a sell-off in stock markets around the world.
Echoing comments made nearly a year ago, Greenspan said wages could only be held down so long and would ultimately rise.
"The recent pickup in some measures of wages suggest that the transition may be already running its course," he said.
"The important question from a monetary policy point of view is whether prospective labour market conditions will be consistent with the maintenance of satifactory price performance," he said.
Greenspan said the U.S. economy grew about 3 percent last year.
"The economy has retained considerable vigour, with few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions," he said.
Greenspan gave the low inflation rate much of the credit for the economy's continued vigour, arguing that it had helped encourage strong capital investment by companies and longer-range planning.
Inflation has partly been held down by stepped-up U.S. imports, which have acted as a "safety valve" for the economy by helping to satisfy domestic demand, he said.
But the main reason for the low inflation rate, according to Greenspan, is subdued wage growth brought on by heightened job insecurity.

Greenspan acknowledged that other factors may have played a role in keeping inflation down, but he tended to discount their importance. They include the sharp slowdown in health care costs, the declining influence of unions, increased foreign competition and stepped-up domestic deregulation.

In setting interest rate policy, the central bank needs to take account not of economic conditions now, but those likely to prevail in six months to a year, or even further ahead, Greenspan said. That is because interest rate changes take time to work their way through the economy.
Greenspan, who jolted global stock markets in December when he warned of the dangers of "irrational exuberance," said in his summary that "the stock market continued to climb at a breathtaking rate."
In answers to questions, Greenspan defended his "irrational exuberance" comment as part of an attempt to explain how developments in asset markets figure into monetary policy decisions.
"It was not a shot from hip," Greenspan said. "We thought long and in detail that any such statement could very well have immediate market effects."
He said he was encouraged by signs that Americans appear to be investing more of their income, saying they may finally be setting aside money needed for retirement.
The Fed chief stressed the importance of increased U.S. savings for the economy as a whole. "Attaining a higher national savings rate quite soon is crucial," he said.
To help boost the national savings rate, Greenspan urged the lawmakers to balance the federal budget and eventually move it into surplus.

As he has done before, Greenspan threw his support behind those who argue that the consumer price index overstates inflation. The evidence, he said, is that inflation has been slower and economic growth faster than government data suggest.
